clue.text: Row in resort, the last thing resort needs

parts.note: a spa is a health resort, such as a spa town

indicators.note: the last thing of a word is its final letter, here taken from the second resort

explanation.surface: A quarrel breaks out at a holiday resort, the last thing such a place wants.
explanation.definitionFit: A spat is a petty quarrel, and a row is a noisy argument, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Brought up in dirtier dens, going off the rails

indicators.note: going off the rails means getting out of control, so the letters of these two words are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone raised in squalid hovels who ends up going wrong in life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brought up' looks like 'raised as a child' in the surface, but here it means dug up from the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Something disinterred has been exhumed, dug up out of the earth, which is what brought up means here.

clue.text: Meal commercial traveller's obtained beside a street

parts.note: a rep, a sales representative, is a commercial traveller

explanation.surface: A travelling salesman grabs a bite to eat at a place just off the street.
explanation.definitionFit: A repast is a formal word for a meal, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Judge and City politicians meeting where food is served

parts.note: a ref, short for referee, judges a game
EC is the postcode of the City of London, the financial district
Tories are Conservative Party politicians in Britain

explanation.surface: A judge and some City of London politicians gather to talk business.
explanation.walkthrough: The City, with a capital C, is London's financial district, whose postcode begins EC.
explanation.definitionFit: Refectories are dining halls in monasteries and colleges, places where meals are served.

clue.text: What one expects to observe in member of religious group

parts.note: par is the expected standard, as in golf where par is the expected number of strokes
to observe is to see

explanation.surface: Musing on what you would expect to notice about a follower of some faith.
explanation.definitionFit: A Parsee is a follower of Zoroastrianism in India, so a member of a religious community.

clue.text: Distinguished cricketer at university recovers from bender

parts.note: Sir Garfield Sobers, the great West Indies all-rounder
up means in residence at university, as in 'up at Oxford'

explanation.surface: A famous cricketer, still a student, nurses a hangover after a big night.
explanation.walkthrough: Garry Sobers is often named as cricket's finest all-rounder; 'up' for at university is a British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: A bender is a drinking spree, and to sober up is to recover from one by losing drunkenness.

clue.text: Successive notes coming from French artist

parts.note: do and re are the first two notes of the sol-fa scale, following one after the other
do and re are the first two notes of the sol-fa scale, following one after the other

explanation.surface: A couple of musical notes drift out from a French painter's studio.
explanation.definitionFit: Gustave Doré was a French illustrator and engraver, famous for his Bible and Dante pictures.

clue.text: Follow academic master as a matter of belief

parts.note: to dog someone is to follow them closely
MA, Master of Arts, is an academic degree

explanation.surface: Taking a professor's word as gospel, simply following the master.
explanation.definitionFit: Dogma is doctrine laid down as settled truth, a body of belief held without question.

clue.text: Journey taking in good mountain feature

indicators.note: taking in means absorbing, so the journey word wraps around the other letter

parts.note: a ride is a journey, as on a horse or bus

explanation.surface: A trip that includes a fine view of the hills.
explanation.definitionFit: A ridge is a long narrow crest of high ground, a typical feature of mountains.

clue.text: Revolutionary, tedious person from what we hear

indicators.note: what we hear signals that the word for the bore is said aloud and spelt differently

parts.note: a pain is an annoying, wearisome person

explanation.surface: A rebel dismissed as a crashing bore, judging by the gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Paine wrote Common Sense and backed both the American and French revolutions.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Paine was a radical pamphleteer of the American Revolution, a revolutionary thinker and activist.

clue.text: Sack group of soldiers — that lot can go to blazes!

definitions.text: that lot can go to blazes!
definitions.note: a noun phrase: the crew who rush off to fires

parts.note: to sack someone is to fire them from a job
a brigade is a military unit of several battalions

explanation.surface: Someone fed up with a troop of soldiers wants them all gone, to hell with them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go to blazes' sounds like a curse but literally means attend fires.
explanation.definitionFit: Firefighters are the people whose job is attending blazes, so the curse is literally their duty.

clue.text: Time to get ready-to-eat food

parts.note: fruit that is ripe is ready to eat

explanation.surface: An announcement that the meal is finally ready.
explanation.definitionFit: Tripe is the stomach lining of cattle, eaten as a dish, so a kind of food.

clue.text: Church always wanting newspaper article? I'll drum up support

definitions.note: spoken by the person, so it stands for a noun

parts.note: e'er is a poetic contraction of ever, meaning always
a leader is a newspaper's editorial article

explanation.surface: The Church perpetually lacks a newspaper piece, so someone offers to rally backing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wanting' looks like 'lacking', a deletion signal, but nothing is removed: it only joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheerleader whips up enthusiasm for a team, so the person who rouses backing speaks the definition.

clue.text: Fantastic sermon, gents being spellbound?

indicators.note: fantastic means fanciful and unreal, so the letters of the next two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A wonderful sermon has the gentlemen in the congregation enthralled.
explanation.definitionFit: Engrossment is the state of total absorption, much like being held as if under a spell.

clue.text: Camels in divine house, one of twelve outside capital

indicators.note: outside means surrounding, so the divine and the house go round the capital

parts.note: DD, Doctor of Divinity, stands for a divine, a clergyman
Rome is the capital of Italy
Aries is one of the twelve astrological houses of the zodiac

explanation.surface: Camels kept in a holy building, one of a dozen standing beyond the capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Divine' is a noun here, a clergyman, abbreviated DD; ROME sits between the two Ds.
explanation.definitionFit: Dromedaries are one-humped camels, the Arabian species.

clue.text: Irish turning up to celebrate historical event in Dublin

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means read from bottom to top, so the abbreviation is backwards

parts.note: to sing is to celebrate in song, as in singing someone's praises

explanation.surface: Irish people turn out to mark a famous anniversary in their capital.
explanation.walkthrough: The Easter Rising of 1916 was a rebellion in Dublin against British rule.
explanation.definitionFit: The Easter Rising of 1916 is the famous insurrection in Dublin, often called simply the Rising.

clue.text: Travel with friends, finally have a little drink and chat

parts.note: to go is to travel

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word friends

parts.note: a sip is a small mouthful of drink

explanation.surface: A day out with mates, a small tipple and a natter.
explanation.definitionFit: Gossip is idle talk about other people, a form of chat.

clue.text: Wild cat, coolest possibly when avoiding sun

indicators.note: possibly says these letters could be arranged another way
avoiding means keeping clear of, so that letter is dropped from the word

explanation.surface: A wild cat that might be the coolest of all when it keeps out of the sunshine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'avoiding' drops S from COOLEST, leaving COOLET for 'possibly' to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The ocelot is a spotted wild cat of Central and South America.

clue.text: Operators getting on in leaps and bounds

indicators.note: in places the small word within the word for leaps

parts.note: surges are sudden rushes forward, like leaps and bounds

explanation.surface: Telephone operators progressing rapidly in their careers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Operators' suggests switchboard staff, but the definition means those who perform operations.
explanation.definitionFit: Surgeons perform operations, so in a medical sense they are operators.

clue.text: Wicked predator shows little sign of sorrow

indicators.note: wicked suggests twisted or bent, so the letters of the hunter word are jumbled

explanation.surface: A cruel hunter shows barely any remorse.
explanation.definitionFit: A single tear falling from the eye is a small outward signal of grief.

clue.text: Good person came down, not at all relaxed

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for saint, a good person
rain came down, so it rained

explanation.surface: A kindly person descended the stairs looking very tense.
explanation.definitionFit: Strained means tense and anxious, the opposite of relaxed.

clue.text: See humour shown by this gathering of emotionally connected folk

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or see
vein means mood or humour, as in 'in a jocular vein'

explanation.surface: An invitation to notice the wit on display at a group of close-knit people.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 'humour' and 'vein' carry the old sense of temper or mood.
explanation.definitionFit: A love-in was a 1960s hippie gathering celebrating love, so a meeting of affectionate people.

clue.text: Cane giving sound of hard blow — we don't like that!

parts.note: bam imitates the noise of a heavy blow
boo is the jeer of a disapproving crowd

explanation.surface: A schoolroom caning lands with a thwack while the class jeers its disapproval.
explanation.definitionFit: Bamboo is a giant grass whose hollow woody stems are used as canes.

clue.text: A president's out of order — they must take steps

indicators.note: out of order means not arranged properly, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A head of state has behaved unacceptably, so action is needed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take steps' seems to mean take action, but it is literal: walking.
explanation.definitionFit: Pedestrians go on foot, so they literally have to walk step by step.

clue.text: Mathematician establishing new rule about transcendental number

indicators.note: about means around, so the rearranged letters surround the number
new signals a fresh arrangement of the letters of rule

parts.note: e, the base of natural logarithms, is a transcendental number

explanation.surface: A mathematician sets up a novel law concerning a number that is not algebraic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' turns RULE into EULR, and 'about' wraps that round E.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonhard Euler was an eighteenth-century Swiss mathematician, among the most prolific ever.

clue.text: Precise demand

definitions.meaning: an adjective meaning accurate, exactly right
a verb meaning to require or extract, as in to extract a toll

explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it means accurate; as a verb it means to insist on or extort payment.

clue.text: Watery terrain — hard to find on another planet

indicators.note: on means placed after, so the hard letter comes after the planet in this across answer

parts.note: Mars is a planet other than Earth
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Boggy ground proves hard to come by on another world.
explanation.definitionFit: A marsh is low wet ground, boggy and waterlogged land.

clue.text: Hurry — daughter must be collected, put out of sight

indicators.note: collected means taken in, so the word for hurry gathers up the letter for daughter

parts.note: hie is an old word meaning hurry

explanation.surface: A parent rushes off because the daughter needs collecting, then disappears.
explanation.definitionFit: To hide something is to conceal it, to put it where no one can see.

clue.text: A blur, a sleep, awfully nice

indicators.note: awfully means badly, so these letters are messed up into a new order

explanation.surface: Drifting in a hazy doze is terribly pleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awfully nice' reads as one phrase, but 'awfully' is the anagram signal and 'nice' alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Nice and pleasurable both mean agreeable and enjoyable, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Number with purpose getting a great deal

parts.note: an end is an aim or purpose, as in the ends justify the means

explanation.surface: A digit with a goal secures a lucrative bargain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'great deal' suggests a bargain, but here it means a lot.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'no end' means a lot or very much, as in it helped no end.

clue.text: Left-winger to move faster than 22?

definitions.meaning: a slang term for a Trotskyist or other radical leftist
to go at a jog, quicker than a walker on foot (22 is the pedestrians entry)

explanation.walkthrough: 22 refers to the answer at 22-across, people on foot, who walk rather than jog.
explanation.definitionFit: A Trotskyist is called by that short slang name, and the verb means to run at a slow jog.

clue.text: Grow something that can count as one of the daily five?

definitions.meaning: a verb meaning to shoot up or put out new growth

definitions.text: something that can count as one of the daily five?
definitions.meaning: a Brussels vegetable, one of the five daily portions of fruit and veg advised for health

explanation.walkthrough: 'Five a day' is the British health advice to eat five portions of fruit and vegetables daily.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to begin growing; as a noun it is a small green Brussels vegetable.
